Midterms: Democrats retake the House and, according to NBC, the Senate, and Wall Street takes a hit

On the evening of 3 November, NBC News projects that Democrats win the House and the Senate, which would deprive Donald Trump of his Congress in January. Nasdaq 100 futures fell about 2%, the 10-year yield declined and the dollar lost ground [1][5][6].
NBC News projects that Democrats win the House of Representatives and the Senate; they needed a net gain of three seats in the House and four in the Senate, where Republicans held 53 of 100 [1][4].

In the House, estimates range from about 244 to 248 Democratic seats, against 218 needed for a majority. Hakeem Jeffries wrote "Victory for America!" and is due to become Speaker of the House when the session opens on 3 January [2].

In the Senate, Democrats flip Texas (James Talarico beats Attorney General Ken Paxton), North Carolina (Roy Cooper beats Michael Whatley), Ohio (Sherrod Brown beats Jon Husted), South Carolina (Annie Andrews) and Iowa (Josh Turek beats Ashley Hinson) [3][4]. Maine and Alaska have not yet been decided [3].
In the markets, S&P 500 futures lost about 1.1 to 1.3% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 2%, as investors feared Democrats would slow the construction of AI data centers [5][6].
The 10-year yield fell by almost 5 basis points, to 4.902%, and the dollar index declined 0.32% [5][7].

Before the vote, Donald Trump told CBS News: "if we didn't win, I'd veto everything." That same evening, he told the New York Times he accepted the results and wanted to "work with the Democrats" [8][9].
Key takeaway: for the first time in Trump's second term, Congress stops being a mere relay. A Democratic House can launch investigations and refuse the bills the president asks for [2].

On tariffs, the change is real but limited. Jeffries wants to "restore Congress's authority" on the matter, but Trump has promised a veto: without a very large majority, a bill against his tariffs has little chance of becoming law. The likely effect: symbolic votes, not a quick reversal [2][8].

Markets reacted mostly to AI, not to tariffs. Goldman Sachs judges that a Democratic Congress could cut tax breaks for these data centers, but that a national moratorium remains unlikely [6]. The drop in yields, for its part, reflects the expectation of a gridlocked Congress, and therefore less fiscal stimulus [5].

Caution: these are projections, and two Senate races remain open. Since 1950, the S&P 500 was higher twelve months after each of the 19 midterm elections (+15% on average, according to FXStreet), with no guarantee [7].

If you are in Europe, US tariffs will not fall overnight: Trump keeps his veto. If your savings follow global funds or US ETFs, tech and AI weigh heavily in them, and they are what wobbled the most. We do not say whether to buy or sell.

Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday 1 November without a deal. An official told Reuters this was not due to difficulties in the talks, and that a draft text was circulating [6].

This draft takes up the seven-step plan presented by Iran in September: an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports, reopening of Hormuz to commercial traffic, a waiver for Iranian oil sales, cancellation of new sanctions, then later talks [6].

Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran on Monday evening. A senior Iranian official told Reuters the two sides remained far from a deal. Tehran demands the lifting of oil sanctions, an end to the naval blockade and the release of frozen funds before reopening the strait [3].
Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei says he has cut the plan's implementation period from seven to two days, but "everything depends" on Washington accepting his demands.

Key takeaway: the Strait of Hormuz remains closed in practice, and every military incident or diplomatic signal moves the oil price within hours. The blockade affects about 20% of the world's oil supply [5].

The sticking point is a question of sequence: Iran wants the lifting of the blockade and sanctions and the thawing of its funds first, and only then talks on the nuclear issue. Washington, for its part, keeps up military pressure while the mediators work.

Both tracks are moving at the same time. Iranian sources cited by Reuters consider a new US attack more likely than a deal, and market concern focuses on the period after 3 November, once the US vote has passed [3][5]. For Europe and Asia, big importers of Gulf energy, a deal would bring prices down, and a failure would push them back up [5].

Egypt: Banque du Caire lists on the stock exchange and brings the state more than $650 million

On Monday 2 November, Banque du Caire made its debut on the Egyptian stock exchange after the sale of 45% of its capital at 5.30 pounds per share. The operation brings more than $650 million to Banque Misr, its state-owned parent, and revives the privatization program demanded by the IMF [1][2][4].
The final IPO price was set at 5.30 Egyptian pounds per share, the top of the range. This values the bank at about 80.83 billion pounds, or $1.46 billion [4].
This covers 6.86 billion shares, or 45% of the capital, versus 30% initially announced. All are existing shares: the money goes to Banque Misr, the state shareholder, and not to Banque du Caire [4].

The proceeds reach about 36.4 billion pounds, more than $650 million. According to EnterpriseAM, it is the biggest IPO on the Cairo exchange in at least ten years; EFG Hermes, one of the organizers, calls it the second-largest privatization via the stock exchange in the country's history [2][3].

Demand exceeded supply: the offering was oversubscribed about six times, according to Ecofin [4]. Two foreign public investors also took stakes: the International Finance Corporation (IFC, World Bank) is investing $100 million and the EBRD the same amount, or 6.9% of the capital for the latter [5].
The stock, listed under the ticker BQDC, climbed as much as 7% in its first session, according to Reuters [6].

Prime Minister Moustafa Madbouly welcomed the government's commitment to "continue its state asset divestment program." A senior official cited by EnterpriseAM says the Treasury will take up to half of the proceeds to ease pressure from public debt [3].

Key takeaway: Egypt needs dollars and proof that it is reforming. Selling part of a state bank brings in foreign currency and shows investors that privatizations are finally moving forward, after years of delays [3][6].

Under its IMF program, Cairo has committed to selling stakes in more than 30 state-owned companies [3]. The IPO had been discussed since 2007 and was postponed several times, notably because of the pandemic and the wars in Ukraine and Gaza [6].

The state nonetheless keeps control: Banque Misr retains 55% of Banque du Caire [4]. Investors are therefore buying a stake in a state bank, not a privatized bank. AGBI's analysis presented the operation as a test of the country's privatization plans [7].
The context remains tense: the war in the Gulf, which weighs on the Suez Canal and on energy, did not prevent demand from staying strong, as the bank had anticipated in October [7].

If you follow Egypt, a neighbor of Europe across the Mediterranean and gateway to the Suez Canal, this operation shows whether the country can attract capital without a new debt crisis. It changes nothing for your savings in France.

Malawi: no dollars, no more fuel. The president returns home amid a shortage

Malawi no longer has enough foreign currency to pay for its fuel: queues lasting several days, reluctant foreign banks, an IMF deal stalled. President Peter Mutharika returned around 1 November, after almost a month in South Africa [1][2][6].
The country consumes about two million liters of fuel a day, which requires about $49 million in foreign currency a month, according to the national oil company cited by Africanews [1].
Foreign banks are hesitating to confirm letters of credit, the payment guarantees without which suppliers do not deliver. Some sellers demand to be paid in advance [1][3].
A truck drivers' union official describes vehicles spending up to a week in queues. In Blantyre, two of fifteen stations visited had gasoline, with queues up to 400 meters long [1].

The government has sought emergency financing, including selling gold from its reserves. It also points to logistical problems linked to unrest after the election in Tanzania, through which part of the fuel passes [1].
The IMF left the country in June 2026 without a new program; the previous one, worth $175 million, ended in May 2025 after only $35 million had been disbursed [4].

The IMF wants a more flexible kwacha. Finance Minister Joseph Mwanamvekha rules out a devaluation, as it would solve nothing without more foreign currency. Malawi24 had nonetheless headlined on 7 October that the president "agrees" to devalue; the government denies it [4][5][8].
Peter Mutharika returned from South Africa around 1 November. He acknowledges fuel difficulties, but attributes them to transport [6].
Key takeaway: the gasoline shortage is first of all a dollar shortage. The country imports its fuel and pays for it in foreign currency; without it, trucks, taxis and factories stop [1][2].

The official kwacha rate is about 1,749 to the dollar, but the parallel market has seen gaps of up to 150% in March 2025, according to the IMF. The bigger the gap, the more importers prefer the black market and the more the state runs short of foreign currency [4].

The war in the Middle East worsens the problem: more expensive oil raises the bill for a country with almost nothing in reserve [1]. There is a precedent: in 2012, Malawi devalued its currency by a third, a shock that pushed prices up [9].
The dilemma is political as much as economic. Devaluing would raise the price of everything imported, but refusing prolongs the shortages and blocks IMF aid [4][5].

Malawi is far from France, but the story is the same as in other poor countries: when oil rises, it is countries without foreign-exchange reserves that suffer first, then their neighbors through migration and prices.

Argentina: country risk jumps to 829 points and the dollar hits a record, markets hold their breath ahead of the US verdict

On 3 November, Argentina's country risk as measured by JP Morgan rose to 829 points, its highest since the October 2025 elections, while the wholesale dollar hit a nominal record. Investors fear the US midterm elections will reduce Washington's support for Javier Milei [1][2].

Country risk, which measures the gap between what Argentina pays to borrow in dollars and what the United States pays, gained 24 points (3%) in one session, to 829 basis points according to the JP Morgan indicator. It has doubled since its floor of 403 points on 7 July [1][2].
The wholesale dollar reached a new nominal high, around 1,551 pesos according to a local outlet [3].
Argentine dollar bonds and Argentine stocks listed on Wall Street fell to their lowest levels in a year, according to Infobae [1].

Analysts fear that a defeat for Donald Trump's camp in the US Congress would reduce his room to maneuver to help Buenos Aires [5][7].

Washington has opened a $20 billion swap line (currency exchange) with Argentina; the decision rests with the US Treasury, without a vote in Congress [7]. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Treasury was ready to buy Argentine dollar bonds if the situation required it [6].

Key takeaway: Argentina pays more to borrow because investors doubt two things at once, the level of dollars in reserve at the central bank and the duration of US support. On the day of the US vote, these two doubts added up [1][5].

The mechanism is simple. When country risk rises, the Argentine state finds it harder to borrow on international markets, while dollar maturities await it in the coming years. Infobae attributes the pressure to the weakness of net reserves against these maturities and to savers' demand for dollars, which pushes the rate up [1].

The government is trying to distance itself from the US vote, but dependence on Donald Trump remains at the center of the debate, notes the Argentine outlet Infocielo [8]. The sources consulted do not yet give the result of the US vote: the market can therefore move quickly in either direction.

Colombia: government warns of a payment default in 2027 if Congress rejects its fiscal rescue bill

The mechanism: when spending durably exceeds revenue, the state borrows more and pays more interest, which widens the deficit further. With 155 trillion pesos of annual debt service, the government wants to act on both spending and taxes [8]. According to the government, seven pesos of adjustment out of ten would come from spending cuts, reduced bureaucracy and the sale of unneeded assets [11].

The head of government and eight ministers resigned from the House of Representatives, because a seat as a member of parliament is incompatible with a ministerial post [2].

For a newly formed executive, it is also a political message: the high cost of living is the first social demand, and the response comes within the first weeks [1][3].
